**On Desire Paths**

There is a strip of dead grass behind almost every building where people gather. You know the one. The architect laid down a concrete walk that meets the parking lot at a tidy right angle, and beside it, cutting the corner at exactly the angle the concrete refuses to take, there is a brown groove worn into the lawn. In dry weather it is packed hard as a floor. In wet weather it becomes a small canal of mud that people step through anyway, ruining their shoes, because the alternative is to walk an extra thirty feet in a direction they do not want to go.

Planners call these *desire paths*, or sometimes *desire lines*. The phrase is often attributed to Gaston Bachelard, the French philosopher of space and reverie, though nobody seems able to find the passage where he actually says it, and I have come to suspect the attribution is itself a kind of desire path—a shortcut people take toward a plausible source because the real route is too long to walk. It doesn't matter much. The term is good regardless of its parentage. It says something true: that a path is a record of wanting. Every worn line in the grass is a vote, cast in footsteps, for a route that someone with authority declined to build.

I find them moving in a way I have trouble explaining. Part of it is the sheer legibility. Most of what people want is invisible or contested or hidden behind what they say they want. But a desire path is want made physical, accumulated, impossible to fake. Nobody walks across a lawn to make a political point. They do it because they're late, or because it's raining, or because the human body, left to itself, does not like right angles. Ten thousand small acts of impatience, none of them meant as communication, add up to a message so clear you could pave it.

And sometimes people do. There's a story—told about Michigan State, about Ohio State, about Virginia Tech, about half a dozen other campuses, which is usually a sign the story is at least partly folklore—that the administration once refused to lay any sidewalks between the new buildings until a year had passed. They waited, watched where the students actually walked, and then poured concrete along the trails that had appeared. Whether or not any given university really did this, it is documented that groundskeepers in Helsinki have used a version of the technique in city parks: they wait for the first heavy snowfall and then go out to photograph the footprints. The snow holds the evidence for a few hours before it gets churned, and in those hours the park reveals how it is actually used, as opposed to how it was drawn.

I like the snow version better than the campus version, because it admits that the evidence is perishable. You have to be looking at the right moment. Most desire paths are not so obliging. They form over years, and by the time they're deep enough to notice, the person who designed the original layout has often moved on, and the person who maintains it has an incentive not to see them. Groundskeepers plant hedges across them. Facilities departments put up small chains or those little wire hoops with signs asking you, please, to keep off. And the path reappears three feet to the left, because a hedge can redirect a want but cannot abolish it.

---

Once you have the concept, you start to see it everywhere, which is the mark of either a genuinely useful idea or a very sticky one. I think it's the former, mostly.

Language is the great field of desire paths. Every grammatical rule is a sidewalk laid by someone with a plan, and every "error" that thousands of people make in the same direction is a trail worn beside it. *Irregardless* is a desire path. So is *could care less*, which everyone agrees is illogical and which everyone understands anyway, because logic was never the point; the point was to get from one side of the sentence to the other with the least effort and the most emphasis. The word *you* is a desire path so deep it has become the only road. Once English had *thou* for one person and *you* for several or for someone you were being polite to, and over a few centuries speakers simply stopped taking the *thou* route, until the sidewalk cracked and grass grew through it and now the old path survives only in prayers and in the speech of a few Quakers and in a certain kind of fantasy novel.

Linguists have a lovely name for one version of this process: *grammaticalization*. A phrase that started as ordinary content—*going to*, meaning literally moving toward a place—gets used so often in a particular way that it wears down into a grammatical tool. *I'm going to the store* still has legs and a destination. *I'm going to think about it* has neither; *going to* has become a future tense marker, and in speech it has worn further still, into *gonna*, a smooth channel with none of the original meaning left in its walls. Nobody decided this. No committee met. People just kept walking that way, and the language, which is only the sum of where people walk, adjusted.

The purists who object to these paths are not wrong to notice them. They are only wrong about what the noticing means. A prescriptive grammarian standing over *irregardless* with a clipboard is exactly the groundskeeper putting up a chain. He is not defending the lawn. He is defending the drawing of the lawn.

---

Software has its own version, and it is the one that has taught me most about the strange relationship between designers and the designed-for.

In August of 2007, a man named Chris Messina posted a message on Twitter suggesting that people use the pound sign to group related messages: *how do you feel about using # (pound) for groups*. Twitter, the company, did not think much of it. The people who ran the service reportedly considered it too nerdy, the sort of thing programmers would like and nobody else. But users started doing it anyway, first a handful and then a great many, especially during a set of wildfires in San Diego a few months later when people needed to find one another's reports in the noise. Within two years Twitter had hyperlinked hashtags automatically. Within five, the symbol had escaped the platform entirely and was appearing on television, on protest signs, on the sides of buses. The path was worn so deep that it became the road, and then the road became the map.

The @-mention has a similar history. So does the retweet, which people were doing by hand—copying a message, typing *RT* in front of it—for a long time before there was a button. If you look at almost any piece of software that has been used by real people for long enough, you find a layer of these worn grooves: keyboard shortcuts nobody documented, spreadsheets used as databases, a "notes" field used to store the thing the form should have had a proper field for. Each one is a small monument to a gap between what the designer imagined and what the world needed. Each is, in a sense, a complaint that nobody bothered to file, because filing it would have taken longer than just walking across the grass.

The best designers I have read about treat these grooves as gifts. They are free research, conducted at scale, by people with no incentive to lie. The worst treat them as vandalism. What separates the two attitudes is not intelligence but a certain humility about the drawing—a willingness to believe that the plan was a hypothesis and the footprints are the data.

---

And yet. I want to be careful here, because the idea is seductive enough to become a slogan, and slogans are their own kind of paved road that stops you from thinking.

Not every desire path deserves to be paved. Some of them cut through things that matter. In alpine meadows, a single social trail—the hikers' term for a desire path—can take decades to heal, because the plants at that elevation grow so slowly that a few summers of footsteps erase a century of growth. The official trail, the one that switchbacks tediously up the slope instead of going straight at it, is not a failure of the designer to understand what hikers want. The designer understands perfectly well what hikers want. The trail is built against that want, on purpose, because the want, satisfied, would destroy the very thing the hikers came for.

The same is true of some rules of language. The distinction between *fewer* and *less* is pedantic and nobody needs it, fine. But the distinction between *imply* and *infer* carries real information that gets lost when the two are merged, and the fact that many people merge them is a desire path worth at least a small chain and a polite sign. Some friction is load-bearing. The trick—and it is a trick, not a principle, because it has to be performed freshly each time—is telling the difference between friction that protects something and friction that merely protects the drawing.

There is also the uncomfortable question of *whose* desire the path records. A trail across a campus lawn is democratic in the simplest possible sense: everybody's foot weighs about the same. But most systems are not lawns. When a piece of software develops a worn groove, it is worn by the users who are already there, who already have the patience to find the workaround. The people who gave up at the front door leave no footprints at all. If you pave only the paths you can see, you build a city for the people who were already able to walk in it. This is a real limitation of the whole way of thinking, and the Helsinki gardeners photographing snow are not immune to it: the snow records the people who go to the park in winter.

So I hold the idea a little loosely. Desire paths are evidence, and evidence is not the same as a verdict. What they do reliably is expose the gap—the distance between the plan and the use—and put it where you cannot pretend not to see it. What you do about the gap is still up to you.

---

I have been circling something more personal, and I might as well walk straight at it.

Writing feels like this to me. Any subject is a field, and somewhere across it there is a paved route: the obvious argument, the five-paragraph structure, the way this sort of essay is supposed to go. And there is also, always, a diagonal—a thing you actually want to say that the paved route doesn't quite reach, so you find yourself stepping off the concrete and onto the grass, hoping it's not too muddy, hoping the groundskeeper isn't watching.

The first time you take the diagonal, it looks like an error. The sentence runs a little long; the paragraph goes somewhere the outline didn't sanction; you use a word that is not quite the right word but is the word that gets you there. The tenth time, it's a habit. The hundredth, it's a style. Every writer I love has a set of these worn grooves, routes they take again and again because their thinking runs that way, and you can trace them through the work like footprints in snow: the sentence that turns on a semicolon and doubles back, the paragraph that ends a beat early, the refusal to summarize at the end. Style is just the accumulated record of where a mind wanted to go when the road didn't go there.

The Latin phrase is *solvitur ambulando*—it is solved by walking. It's usually told as a joke about Diogenes, who, when someone argued that motion was impossible, got up and walked away. But I've always heard something gentler in it too. Some problems can't be solved from the drawing. You have to get out onto the ground and walk, and the walking is the thinking, and the path you make while thinking is the only honest record of the thought. An essay that goes exactly where its outline said it would go has proven that the outline was correct. It has not necessarily found anything out.

This is not an argument against outlines, any more than the lawn is an argument against sidewalks. It's an argument for looking down occasionally to see where your feet have actually been going, and for taking that seriously as information. The route you keep drifting toward is trying to tell you something about where you want to arrive. Sometimes the right response is to pave it. Sometimes the right response is a chain and a polite sign. But the wrong response—the only wrong response—is to insist that the grass is undisturbed when anyone with eyes can see the mud.

---

I'll end where I started, on the lawn behind the building.

It's late afternoon in my imagination of it, that hour when the light comes in flat and every irregularity in the ground throws a shadow. The paved walk goes off to the right at its confident angle. The desire path cuts left, brown and slightly sunken, and someone is walking on it right now—not thinking about desire or design or anything at all, just going home. They step over the wet part. Where the trail meets the pavement there's a little fan of dried mud that hundreds of shoes have carried out of the grass and deposited on the concrete, so that even the official route bears the mark of the unofficial one. Nobody planned that either.

There is a dignity in this that I don't want to overstate but also don't want to miss. The person on the path is not rebelling. They have no theory. They're just declining, in the most ordinary way possible, to pretend that the shortest distance between where they are and where they want to be is anything other than a straight line. And the ground, which has no opinions about anything, is keeping the record for them—patiently, in mud and dead grass, one footprint at a time—in case anyone with a clipboard ever decides to look down and read it.
